paragraphs: Structured output learning predicts outputs whose parts have meaningful relationships. This paper approaches that problem through regression, extending kernel dependency estimation with operator-valued kernels. The formulation addresses two restrictions of the original approach: treating outputs separately in the transformed space and being unable to use a joint feature space.

The authors first construct a kernel using covariance, which describes how outputs vary together. This lets the method represent interactions within the output feature space. However, those interactions alone do not account for the inputs. A second construction uses conditional covariance to incorporate both relationships among outputs and the effects of input variables.

The distinction matters because output relationships and input-dependent relationships offer different information for prediction. The paper evaluates both constructions on three structured output problems and compares them with existing kernel-based regression methods. The abstract establishes the expanded modeling framework and the scope of evaluation, without claiming that either construction consistently wins.
icml-2013-a-generalized-kernel-approach-.tldr: An expanded kernel regression framework models relationships among structured outputs and, through conditional covariance, their dependence on inputs.

paragraphs: Kernels provide a way to compare structured objects for learning. Many kernels for discrete structures come from convolution kernels or their broader mapping-kernel framework. That framework is attractive because it provides criteria for checking positive definiteness and supports efficient computation through dynamic programming. These properties make mathematically valid comparisons easier to construct and use.

The paper argues that familiar kernels occupy only a small part of what this framework permits. Building on the theory of partitionable kernels, it identifies a previously unexplored class and gives a mathematical characterization of it. This turns an open design opportunity into a defined family of possible kernels.

The authors then use that characterization to develop a parameterized way of adapting kernels in the class to particular problems. Their experiments suggest that the resulting kernels are promising in both accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution therefore combines a broader mathematical design space with a practical way to search within it, rather than presenting only one fixed similarity function.
icml-2013-a-new-frontier-of-kernel-desig.tldr: The paper characterizes a new class of structured-data kernels and develops a parameterized method for adapting them to specific problems.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning chooses how to combine kernels while also learning a predictor from that combination. When there are extremely many candidate kernels, even work proportional to their number can become impractical. This paper develops randomized mirror descent for an empirical-risk objective with a group p-norm penalty.

Its central idea is to estimate gradients cheaply while keeping their variance low. The authors use importance sampling and identify an ideal distribution that selects each coordinate with probability proportional to its gradient magnitude. For learning polynomial-kernel coefficients, the combinatorial organization of the base kernels makes sampling from this distribution possible in O(log(d)) time.

In that polynomial-kernel setting, the stated total cost of reaching an epsilon-optimal solution is O(log(d)/epsilon²). This is the source of the dramatic improvement in dependence on the number of kernels, rather than a general guarantee for every kernel collection. Experiments on simulated and real data also find the algorithm computationally more efficient than the alternatives considered.
icml-2013-a-randomized-mirror-descent-al.tldr: Importance-sampled mirror descent makes learning certain enormous kernel combinations efficient, with logarithmic dependence on their number in the polynomial-kernel setting.

paragraphs: A classifier can perform well across its full ROC curve while the application cares about only a particular range of false positive rates. Partial AUC measures performance within that range. This paper develops a structural SVM framework that directly targets partial AUC between any two specified false positive rates.

The framework uses a cutting plane solver, which repeatedly finds a constraint that the current solution violates most strongly. For full AUC, the required combinatorial search separates into manageable pieces. Restricting attention to partial AUC makes that decomposition harder, creating a computational obstacle to optimizing the measure that the application actually uses.

The paper's key technical result is an efficient algorithm for this constraint-search problem. Its computational complexity matches the corresponding algorithm for full AUC. This makes the proposed approach practical for a chosen false positive interval without increasing the complexity of that central subproblem. Demonstrations on several real-world tasks support its applicability; the abstract does not claim uniform performance gains.
icml-2013-a-structural-svm-based-approac.tldr: A structural SVM framework efficiently optimizes partial AUC over any specified false positive range.

paragraphs: When designs must satisfy several objectives, there may be no single best choice. Instead, the goal is a Pareto-optimal set: designs offering tradeoffs that cannot be improved in one objective without sacrificing another. Evaluating every candidate can be too expensive, so the paper asks how to identify this set using selective measurements.

The proposed Pareto Active Learning algorithm models the objectives with Gaussian processes. These models capture structure across the design space and accommodate noisy evaluations. PAL uses them to choose the next design to evaluate, aiming to make progress toward predicting the Pareto set while allowing control over accuracy and sampling cost.

The authors provide theoretical bounds on the sampling required for a desired accuracy. On three real-world datasets, PAL also improves significantly over the evolutionary algorithm used for comparison, with savings of about 33% in many cases. These findings support targeted evaluation as a way to reduce the expense of discovering useful tradeoffs, rather than exhaustively testing the design pool.
icml-2013-active-learning-for-multi-obje.tldr: Pareto Active Learning selectively evaluates designs to identify good multi-objective tradeoffs with controlled accuracy and sampling cost.

paragraphs: Crowdsourced classification collects labels from people, but human mistakes and spam make those labels unreliable. A common response is to ask several workers about each instance and combine their answers. This paper examines another part of the process: deciding which classification tasks should be assigned to which workers.

The authors study assignment together with label inference for heterogeneous tasks. Their algorithm adapts assignments as work proceeds, using online primal-dual optimization techniques. The resulting method has a provable near-optimality guarantee. The contribution is therefore a principled allocation procedure, connecting decisions about collecting labels with the eventual task of predicting the correct labels.

The stated finding is that adaptive assignment can improve prediction accuracy while reducing cost when the available workers are diverse. That qualification matters: the value comes from making better use of differences within the worker population. The paper shows why improving a crowdsourcing system need not depend only on collecting more answers or combining existing answers more cleverly.
icml-2013-adaptive-task-assignment-for-c.tldr: A provably near-optimal adaptive assignment algorithm can improve crowdsourced classification accuracy at lower cost when workers are diverse.

paragraphs: Deep belief networks are known to approximate arbitrary distributions over fixed-length binary vectors, but their ability to represent real-valued data requires a separate analysis. This paper studies networks with two binary hidden layers and visible variables whose conditional distributions belong to the exponential family.

Under mild assumptions, these networks can represent additive mixtures of exponential-family distributions with independent variables within each component. More precisely, an m-dimensional mixture with n components can be approximated arbitrarily closely in Kullback-Leibler divergence using m visible variables and hidden layers of sizes n and n+1. This connects the size of a mixture representation to an explicit network architecture.

The analysis also covers relevant infinite mixtures, showing that finite networks can approximate them arbitrarily well. One stated case involves fixed-variance Gaussian mixtures restricted to a compact domain, which can themselves approximate any strictly positive density there. These are representational results: they establish what suitably chosen network parameters can express, rather than reporting the outcome of a training experiment.
icml-2013-approximation-properties-of-db.tldr: Under stated assumptions, two-hidden-layer binary DBNs can approximate broad families of real-valued mixture distributions with explicit network-size guarantees.

paragraphs: Optimizing long-run average reward requires a system to have well-defined stationary behavior. Under partial observability, the learner cannot directly see the complete state, making the representation of that behavior important. This paper studies the problem using linear predictive state representations, which describe a system through predictions.

The authors show that the stationary distribution is well behaved and depends on policy parameters through a rational function, meaning a ratio of polynomials. They then define a related predictive-state reward process and establish that its average reward is also a rational function of those parameters. The complexity of this expression depends on the dimension of the underlying linear representation.

This connects representation size to the difficulty of searching for a rewarding policy. The results suggest that average-reward policy search can be effective when the predictive representation is small, even if a partially observable Markov decision process description needs many hidden states. Illustrative examples support that possibility; the abstract presents it as a promising consequence rather than a universal efficiency guarantee.
icml-2013-average-reward-optimization-ob.tldr: Small predictive state representations yield structured average-reward objectives that may make policy search effective despite many hidden states.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to learn the structure of an undirected graphical model by maximum likelihood while placing a bound on its treewidth. The bound restricts the graph structures under consideration. Finding the best structure is NP-hard, and many existing approaches rely on local searches through candidate graphs.

The authors formulate the task as a combinatorial optimization problem and then relax it into a convex problem. The relaxed search uses specially structured forest and hyperforest polytopes, geometric sets that encode aspects of the original discrete choices. This provides a different route for tackling the structural search rather than relying solely on local changes to a graph.

A supergradient method solves the dual formulation. The stated cost per iteration is O(k³ n^(k+2) log n), where n counts variables and k bounds treewidth, making the dependence on the structural bound explicit. Comparisons on synthetic data and established benchmarks show gains from the proposed convex approach. These results concern the relaxation-based method, without turning the underlying NP-hard problem into a general exact convex optimization task.
icml-2013-convex-relaxations-for-learnin.tldr: A convex relaxation provides an alternative to local search for learning bounded-treewidth graphical models, with gains in the reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Structured regularization encourages patterns in a learned model, rather than treating every parameter independently. Such objectives can combine components that are awkward to optimize together. This paper develops stochastic optimization methods by combining familiar online learning techniques with the Alternating Direction Multiplier Method, a framework for optimizing composite functions.

The authors propose two online ADMM variants. One corresponds to proximal gradient descent, and the other to regularized dual averaging. Both are described as computationally efficient and straightforward to implement. Their purpose is to bring ADMM's treatment of composite structure into an online optimization setting while retaining theoretical control over learning performance.

Both methods achieve an expected-risk convergence rate of O(1/√T). For a strongly convex loss, the proximal-gradient variant has the faster rate O(log(T)/T). That stronger conclusion belongs to that method and assumption specifically. Numerical experiments demonstrate effectiveness on learning problems with structured sparsity, including overlapping group lasso, connecting the optimization framework to models whose parameter groups can overlap.
icml-2013-dual-averaging-and-proximal-gr.tldr: Two online ADMM methods support structured regularization with convergence guarantees, including a faster rate for one variant under strong convexity.

paragraphs: Pool-based active learning chooses which examples in an available collection should receive labels. This paper studies that problem for halfspaces, classifiers defined by a linear separating boundary. It revisits an aggressive approach and asks whether it can be both computationally practical and supported by theoretical guarantees.

The main analysis concerns the realizable setting, where a suitable classifier can separate the pool correctly. Formal approximation guarantees apply when that separation has a margin. The authors also establish that there are cases in which the aggressive approach needs significantly fewer labels than a mellow approach, giving a theoretical reason to prefer it in some settings.

For pools with a small amount of unavoidable error, the paper introduces a simple heuristic for using the same algorithm. Experiments show substantial label-complexity improvements in both realizable and low-error settings. The distinction between these findings matters: the formal margin-based guarantees concern the realizable analysis, while successful use on low-error pools is supported through the heuristic and experiments.
icml-2013-efficient-active-learning-of-h.tldr: An efficient aggressive active learner can reduce label requirements for halfspaces, with margin-based guarantees and encouraging low-error experiments.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis studies relationships between two sets of variables. This paper focuses on computing it efficiently when the two input matrices are tall and thin. Instead of carrying out the entire calculation on the original matrices, the proposed method first creates smaller versions using randomized dimensionality reduction.

The procedure has two stages: apply the randomized transform, then run a standard CCA algorithm on the resulting pair. This separation is useful because the acceleration comes from reducing the input size. The second stage can use any standard CCA algorithm, so the proposal provides a preprocessing route rather than requiring one particular replacement for the core solver.

The authors prove that the result approximates CCA for the original matrices. They also show that the procedure requires asymptotically fewer operations than the leading exact algorithms considered. The contribution is a mathematically supported tradeoff between exact computation and reduced computational work: the smaller problem produces a guaranteed approximation to the original analysis.
icml-2013-efficient-dimensionality-reduc.tldr: Randomized dimensionality reduction accelerates CCA on tall, thin matrices while providing provable approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Lifelong learning involves learning a sequence of tasks while using experience from earlier ones. This paper introduces ELLA, an online multi-task learning method designed for that setting. Its central challenge is to share useful information across tasks while updating the shared representation as additional tasks arrive.

ELLA maintains a common basis from which individual task models are built, with sparse sharing determining how tasks use that basis. A new task draws on the current basis, and learning then refines the basis with performance across all tasks in mind. This makes the shared representation both a source of transferred knowledge and an object that continues to improve.

The authors connect the method to online dictionary learning for sparse coding and to batch multi-task learning, and provide theoretical performance guarantees. In their experiments, sequential learning achieves nearly the same performance as batch multi-task learning while taking over 1,000 times less time. This is an empirical result supporting the efficiency of the proposed lifelong-learning approach.
icml-2013-ella-an-efficient-lifelong-lea.tldr: ELLA incrementally refines a sparsely shared task basis, achieving near-batch performance with over 1,000-fold less learning time in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons can be represented as a graph: alternatives are vertices, and observed comparisons are edges. Statistical ranking seeks a score for each alternative whose differences agree with those comparisons. This paper asks how the choice of observed pairs affects the information available for estimating that ranking.

The authors propose selecting additional comparisons to maximize the increase in Fisher information. Under certain assumptions, this data-collection task separates into a graph problem: choose a fixed number of edges so that the graph Laplacian's second eigenvalue is as large as possible. The reduction connects a statistical objective to a precise spectral property of the comparison graph.

An application to the Yahoo! Movie user-rating dataset shows that a small number of carefully selected comparisons can substantially increase the ranking's Fisher informativeness. The finding concerns how informative the collected data are for ranking estimation. It supports choosing new comparisons strategically, while the spectral reduction itself remains conditional on the assumptions stated by the authors.
icml-2013-enhanced-statistical-rankings-.tldr: Targeted pairwise comparisons can make rankings more informative, with a conditional reduction of data selection to a graph eigenvalue problem.

paragraphs: In high-dimensional classification, predicting labels accurately and identifying the variables that matter are distinct goals. Existing theory had sharply described classification risk and closeness to a discriminative rule, but those results did not establish equally sharp guarantees for variable selection. The paper addresses this gap, motivated by the importance of interpreting models in scientific applications.

The authors analyze the ROAD estimator and provide sharp sufficient conditions for consistent variable selection. These conditions describe circumstances in which the estimator can reliably identify the relevant variables. Their sufficiency matters: establishing that the conditions support recovery does not make every condition a universal requirement for success.

The paper complements this algorithm-specific result with information-theoretic limits on variable selection. Such limits describe obstacles that cannot simply be removed by choosing a different estimator. Together, the achievable guarantees and necessary limits establish ROAD's optimality for a particular family of problems, giving a more precise account of its feature-selection capabilities than prediction-focused theory alone.
icml-2013-feature-selection-in-high-dime.tldr: Sharp sufficient conditions and information-theoretic limits establish ROAD's variable-selection guarantees and optimality for a particular problem family.

paragraphs: Matrix factorization is a widely used approach to collaborative filtering, but useful auxiliary information can be difficult to incorporate into its predictions. This paper treats that information as features of the factorization and introduces general functional matrix factorization. Conventional matrix factorization models are included as special cases of the proposed formulation.

The authors develop a gradient-boosting algorithm to solve the associated optimization problem efficiently. They also give two specialized algorithms for constructing feature functions for two particular tasks. The central flexibility is that feature functions are learned from training data through a search over an infinite function space, allowing the representation to adapt to the prediction problem.

That flexibility can produce more suitable features and thereby improve prediction accuracy. On three real-world datasets, the proposed method outperforms the baseline methods used in the experiments. The contribution combines a more general modeling formulation with a practical optimization procedure, showing how auxiliary information can become part of the factorization itself.
icml-2013-general-functional-matrix-fact.tldr: General functional matrix factorization uses gradient boosting to learn auxiliary-information features, improving predictions over the reported baselines.

paragraphs: People learn many categories well, but their biological constraints and inductive biases make some classification tasks difficult. This paper asks whether boosting can extend human learning ability. The aim is to obtain better classification performance from human learners on problems that individual people struggle to master.

The authors propose a boosting algorithm for human learners and provide theoretical justification. They test it with Mechanical Turk participants on two synthetic tasks and one real-world task. The synthetic tests include a crosshair problem with a nonlinear decision boundary and a Gabor-patch problem whose boundary is linear but inaccessible to the human learners studied.

The real-world evaluation concerns detecting opinion spam. Across the reported experiments, boosting human learners improves accuracy and overcomes some limitations of individual human learning. The significance is that a task's difficulty for a person does not necessarily determine the performance achievable through a structured learning procedure involving people. The findings support overcoming some constraints, rather than removing human learning limitations generally.
icml-2013-human-boosting-cd28c06a44.tldr: A boosting algorithm for human learners improves classification accuracy and overcomes some individual learning limitations in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A neural associative memory should recover a stored pattern when presented with a corrupted version. It also needs to learn patterns gradually and store many of them without losing retrieval reliability. This paper studies how these three objectives can be achieved together by exploiting redundancy already present in the patterns.

The authors develop an iterative learning algorithm that discovers that redundancy. In their construction, the resulting network has retrieval capacity exponential in network size. The role of redundancy is central: the stated capacity result arises from using structure in the memorized patterns, rather than treating every possible collection of patterns as equally suitable.

The paper also uses local network structure to obtain asymptotic error-correction performance that can scale linearly with network size. Together, these results address storage, incremental learning, and recovery from noise within one framework. The contribution is a way to use shared structure among patterns to avoid the tradeoffs that the authors identify in earlier approaches.
icml-2013-iterative-learning-and-denoisi.tldr: Learning redundancy among stored patterns enables associative memories with exponential retrieval capacity and potentially linear-scaling error correction.

paragraphs: Artificially modifying training examples can expose a predictor to more variation, but explicitly generating and processing many extra examples is costly. This paper proposes marginalized corrupted features, a method that incorporates such variation through an expected loss rather than a large expanded training dataset.

The approach corrupts features using known noise distributions from the exponential family. Training minimizes the loss averaged over the chosen corruption distribution. In this sense, it learns from infinitely many possible corrupted versions of the available examples. The distribution remains important: the added variation is the variation represented by that specified corruption process.

Experiments on several datasets show that MCF classifiers can be trained efficiently, may generalize substantially better, and are more robust when features are deleted at test time. These results connect the training objective to practical robustness: a model trained to perform well across feature corruptions can be less dependent on an intact input. The reported generalization gains are empirical possibilities, rather than guaranteed improvements on every dataset.
icml-2013-learning-with-marginalized-cor.tldr: Marginalized corrupted features averages training loss over known noise distributions to efficiently learn predictors with empirically improved robustness.

paragraphs: Sparse regression seeks a model in which only some covariates have nonzero coefficients. Many approaches assume those covariates are completely observed and noise-free, which can fail in high-dimensional applications. This paper addresses noisy and missing covariates, emphasizing that even estimating the noise covariance can be difficult.

The authors develop a simple variant of orthogonal matching pursuit that recovers the support, meaning the set of variables with nonzero coefficients, without knowing the noise covariance. Matching lower bounds establish that its support-recovery rate is minimax optimal for the studied setting. This separates identifying the active variables from first having to characterize the corruption covariance.

When the noise covariance is available, the algorithm also matches the best-known bounds for coefficient recovery measured in ℓ² error. The authors establish minimax optimality for those bounds as well. Alongside these results, they improve performance guarantees for standard OMP with Gaussian noise. The paper thus distinguishes what can be recovered without covariance knowledge from the stronger coefficient-recovery guarantees available when that information is supplied.
icml-2013-noisy-and-missing-data-regress.tldr: A modified orthogonal matching pursuit method achieves minimax-optimal support recovery without knowing the covariate-noise covariance.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning learns how an environment changes under actions. In environments described by many features, part of that challenge is identifying which features are relevant to the dynamics. This paper proposes a framework that learns the transition model and selects useful features online.

The central representation is a new factored state-transition model. The authors construct it by predicting how actions change the world, and design the representation to support efficient online learning of relevant features. An online sparse-coding technique performs feature selection in the high-dimensional space, connecting the choice of model inputs to the process of learning action effects.

The paper provides theoretical guarantees for the framework and demonstrates its practicality in both simulated and real robotics domains. The contribution lies in integrating representation, feature selection, and dynamics learning into one online approach. Its stated findings support learning useful transition models in feature-rich settings; the abstract's empirical claim concerns practicality rather than a specified improvement in reward or a numerical speedup.
icml-2013-online-feature-selection-for-m.tldr: A factored transition model and online sparse coding jointly learn action effects and select relevant features for model-based reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimizing a convex function when only T queries to a stochastic first-order oracle are available. Its organizing idea is that the function's growth near its minimum determines the difficulty of optimization. A Tsybakov-like condition expresses that growth in terms of distance from the minimizer.

If growth is at least proportional to distance raised to κ, with κ greater than one, the optimal function-value rate is Θ(T^(-κ/(2κ−2))). The familiar convex rate appears as κ approaches infinity, and the strongly convex rate appears at κ = 2. For values between one and two, the analysis yields even faster rates under the corresponding growth condition.

The paper separately derives the optimal rate for locating the minimizer: Θ(T^(-1/(2κ−2))). Distinguishing location from objective value clarifies two different meanings of optimization accuracy. The same precise rates also characterize active-learning complexity, strengthening a connection between the fields through their use of queries chosen in response to feedback.
icml-2013-optimal-rates-for-stochastic-c.tldr: A local growth condition yields optimal stochastic convex optimization rates and links them to active-learning complexity.

paragraphs: Epileptic activity includes short subclinical bursts as well as full clinical seizures. This paper aims to divide those events into distinct dynamic regimes so their patterns can be studied and compared. Intracranial EEG creates a modeling challenge because patients can have different numbers of electrodes in different locations.

The authors develop a Bayesian nonparametric Markov switching process that shares regimes across varying numbers of channels. Channels can switch regimes asynchronously, and the collection of regimes is not fixed in advance. A switching Gaussian graphical model represents sparse, changing dependencies in the innovations process, the part driving new changes in the channel dynamics.

The paper demonstrates the model's importance for parsing recordings and predicting held-out iEEG data. Its state assignments are described as intuitive and potentially useful for automating parts of clinical seizure analysis. They also enable comparison of subclinical bursts with full seizures. The proposed scientific benefit is a better description of event dynamics; the abstract does not claim to establish the underlying relationship between those event classes.
icml-2013-parsing-epileptic-events-using.tldr: A Bayesian switching model parses correlated iEEG channels into shared dynamic regimes, supporting comparison of subclinical bursts and seizures.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe methods solve constrained convex optimization problems through a sequence of linear subproblems. This paper strengthens and generalizes their primal-dual convergence analysis using duality-gap certificates. These certificates provide a way to assess progress toward optimality, connecting the algorithm's updates with a quantitative measure of remaining error.

The analysis also allows approximate solutions of the linear subproblems and inexact gradients. It is worst-case optimal with respect to the sparsity of the resulting solutions. This matters for settings where a useful answer should involve relatively few components and where exact computations inside every iteration may not be available.

The framework unifies many sparse greedy methods over convex hulls of atomic sets, including cases where those sets are only approximated. The applications encompass structured sparse vectors and matrices, low-rank matrices, permutation matrices, and max-norm bounded matrices. The authors also introduce a framework for convex optimization over matrix factorizations in which each Frank-Wolfe iteration makes a low-rank update.
icml-2013-revisiting-frank-wolfe-project.tldr: A duality-gap framework strengthens Frank-Wolfe guarantees, accommodates approximate computations, and unifies sparse and low-rank optimization methods.

paragraphs: Exact Gaussian process regression has a runtime that grows cubically with the number of data points. That makes its computational cost a serious obstacle for large datasets. This paper addresses scaling in the multidimensional-input setting, where each observation is described by several input variables.

The proposed method uses a projected additive approximation to a multidimensional Gaussian process. Its purpose is to reduce the work required while preserving useful predictive performance. The paper positions this construction as a way to extend practical GP scaling to multidimensional problems, which the authors identify as insufficiently addressed by existing advances.

Tests on several datasets find performance close to that of the naive full Gaussian process at computational costs lower by orders of magnitude. The central result is this observed combination of predictive similarity and substantial savings. It suggests that the approximation can make multidimensional GP regression more practical in the tested settings, with closeness to the full model established empirically rather than stated as a universal guarantee.
icml-2013-scaling-multidimensional-gauss.tldr: Projected additive approximations achieve near-full-GP performance at orders-of-magnitude lower computational cost on the tested multidimensional datasets.
